speaker: kyleyoshida
text: Hello everyone, and thank you to the District Council and staff for inviting us to attend this Council meeting. I'll first start by giving a bit of a brief overview of the work we conducted, as well as our general conclusions before opening up for questions. So, just to start with a bit of background in October of last year, we were contacted by the previous District Director of Planning and Community Services to provide a financial analysis of the village South SAP. Our original report with the development program provided to us at that time concluded that the development would be a net economic benefit to the District of lansdale. However, upon reviewing counselor savages feedback, there were three broad areas that we thought brought up good points and that we tried to address in our addendum. These were number one additional police costs number two lower tax revenue assumptions that incorporate administrative and maintenance costs and therefore better reflect net revenues to the district and then number three confirming the specific development program and construction phasing details in order to clarify any confusion. So the first two points were included in the updated analysis in our. addendum and hopefully clarify that the project will very likely be a net economic benefit for the district, the last point regarding development program specifics is valid and likely should be refined further has a bit of background, typically in our experience, the development process will begin with the developer commissioning or conducting a market feasibility study to assess the market warranted development program for a site. it's likely still worthwhile to pursue this in order to further refine and collectively settle on one specific development program. That being said, our update analysis concluded that from an economic point of view, the project remains a net benefit to the district over a 20 year period. Given the expenses the developers are shouldering it's likely that profit margins for them will be very tight and it may not make sense for them to move forward on a mixed use higher density development. In fact, from a profitability as well as community acceptance point of view, it may make more sense to simply develop a large lower density residential units on the site. To conclude, in a certain sense, Lanceville faces a fairly binary choice in terms of what it wants for the site, as well as broader community. Both of these choices are valid long term visions for the district and depend on community priorities. On one hand, lower density and predominantly large single family residential units, similar to what currently exists in the district. Or, on the other hand, higher residential densities that support a mixed used village core and are able to attract and retain commercial tenants. Just to illustrate and hit home that last point as part of our due diligence process, we spoke to senior management of a major potential grocery company who expressed interest in opening a store in Lanceville and they reconfirmed our impression that substantial population growth would be required before it would make economic sense for them to pursue opening a store in the district. Hopefully this clarifies any questions the district council and staff may have. We are happy to answer any additional questions you might still have and thank you once again for your time.

text: Thank you, Mayor. At yesterday's meeting of the RDN, we had a very good presentation by a deputy director of BC assessment. And I know that that topic's on everybody's mind with the increase, but there's a couple of facts. There was a very good slide presentation. I've asked staff to put that onto our village website. Very good explanation of how the assessments work. If you wanted to appeal your assessment, you had to contact them by January 31st. And there's an actual appeal process through BC assessment, which ends on April 31st. And then after that, if you still don't like it, you can appeal to the BC Supreme Court on an issue of law. What I wasn't clear on is that the assessment that you received on January 1st or thereabouts, that value was actually calculated as of July 31st of last year. So there's six months lag in the actual assessed values, because a chart was prepared, which shows the increase in the values in the last six months. And they are astronomical as well. So that will most likely show up. Well, it will show up in next year's assessments. But it's July 31st when they are capped. An interesting point is the definition of non-market change. Market change is the change that takes place when the value of houses goes up. That's called market change. Non-market change includes such things as new construction, because if you add new houses into an area district, that's going to usually raise the value of all the houses in that area. Demolitions, that would tend to decrease the value in that area. Subdivisions going in, or like new construction, that tends to increase the value of the homes. Zoning changes, where a zone is changed. There might be an upzoning. That will affect the assessment. Boundary extensions or property class changes. So I know that we discuss this sometimes when we're doing our budget. What are the non-market changes that take place in our assessments? To finish up, and I'm sure we've read this or seen this in the news, that in Lanceville, the residential single-family increase for this year was 35%. The commercial assessed value increase was 22%. On Vancouver Island, there was a 75% increase in the single-family sales, single-family house sales from 8,000 in 2020 to 14,000 in 2021. An almost 100% increase in the number of sales. This was the first year in the Assessor's opinion, as far as he can remember, that for sales north of the Malahat, forget Victoria, north of the Malahat, there were 1,000 single-family homes that sold for over $1 million, which he found crazy. But those are the numbers. Thank you.
